title: A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital
subtitle: Liu Tong · Yu Yizheng · The Gardens, Temples, and Historic Sites of Ming Dynasty Beijing
description: Liu Tong (c. 1593–1636), courtesy name Tongren, sobriquet Ge'an, was a native of Macheng, Huguang, and a late Ming literary figure. Yu Yizheng (c. 1597–1636), first named Jilu, courtesy name Sizhi, was a native of Wanping, Shuntian. In the eighth year of the Chongzhen era (1635), the two collaborated to complete the eight-volume A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital, which records in detail over 120 gardens, temples, shrines, and scenic spots in Ming dynasty Beijing, written in a fresh and refined style. This route follows in the footsteps of Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng's Ming dynasty Beijing, exploring those surviving heritage sites.

route.title: A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital: A Cultural Map of 120 Scenic Sites in Ming Beijing
route.intro:
The capital, a place of walls. Yan, a region of the heavens. The capital was anciently the land of Ji, with the sea to its left and the Taihang range to its right.
The birth of A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital has a special story: Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng — one from Huguang, the other a native of Beijing — met in the capital and hit it off immediately, deciding to co-author a gazetteer of Beijing's scenic sites. Every weekend, Yu Yizheng would take Liu Tong on excursions throughout and beyond Beijing city — visiting temples to see ancient stelae, touring gardens to admire flowers and trees, exploring ruins in the outskirts. Yu Yizheng contributed Beijing's 'local knowledge,' while Liu Tong polished it with his beautiful prose. They wrote for three years, their footsteps covering more than 120 scenic sites within and beyond Beijing. The book contains not only descriptions of architecture and scenery but also a wealth of historical anecdotes and folk legends — such as the 'Heavenly Heart Stone' of the Temple of Heaven, the stone lions of Lugou Bridge, and the lilacs of Fayuan Temple. In the eighth year of the Chongzhen era (1635), the book was finally carved and published. Sadly, both authors died young — Liu Tong passed away the following year at just forty-three; Yu Yizheng died the same year at only thirty-nine. Their names, together with this book, remain forever in the lanes and alleyways of Beijing. Let us open A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital and step into that Ming dynasty Beijing, still with its city walls, camel bells, and incense smoke.

stops.title: Stop 1: Temple of Heaven — Where the Son of Heaven Dialogued with Heaven
stops.content: The Temple of Heaven ranks first among the temples and altars in A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital. Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng described every detail of this sacrificial complex with poetic language: 'The Circular Mound Altar has three tiers of steps, surrounded by stone railings.' They particularly noted the Heavenly Heart Stone on the Circular Mound — standing on that round stone and speaking softly, the sound echoes back from all directions, like 'heavenly sound.' 'The altar's design takes its form from heaven.' They also recorded in detail the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests — this triple-eaved circular hall with blue glazed tiles, 'its dome in three layers, covered with blue tiles, symbolizing the color of heaven.' At the winter solstice each year, the emperor held the grand sacrifice to heaven here — Liu Tong wrote: 'The Son of Heaven conducts the rite in person, the hundred officials attend in formation, firewood is lit, smoke rises, fragrance reaches the heavens' — those curling incense smoke connected heaven and earth, ruler and people. Less than thirty years after A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital was published, the Temple of Heaven faced its darkest moment — in 1644, Li Zicheng breached Beijing and the Ming dynasty fell. But the Temple of Heaven survived, as did the words in the book — later Qing emperors continued to sacrifice here until the abdication of the Xuantong Emperor in 1912. The Temple of Heaven is not merely a lone altar — from the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests to the Circular Mound Altar, from the Imperial Vault of Heaven to the Hall of Abstinence, the entire complex is laid out with strict planning,暗合 celestial patterns. 'The number of heaven is nine, the altar has three levels, the steps are in nine flights' — every number echoes the supremely yang number nine. To the south, the Divine Music Office has been the training ground for court sacrificial music and dance since the Ming dynasty, the elegant music still echoing today. The Temple of Heaven was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1998, but Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng had already immortalized it in words more than three hundred years ago as 'the place where man dialogues with heaven.'

stops.title: Stop 2: Imperial Ancestral Temple — The Royal Ancestral Shrine of Left Ancestral Temple, Right Altar of Land and Grain
stops.content: The Imperial Ancestral Temple was where Ming and Qing emperors worshipped their ancestors. According to the ancient system of 'ancestral temple on the left, altar of land and grain on the right,' it is symmetrically positioned to the southeast of the Forbidden City with the Altar of Land and Grain. Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng wrote: 'The Imperial Ancestral Temple lies to the left inside the Chengtian Gate, with the main hall in the center and the寝 hall behind, housing the spirit tablets of successive emperors and empresses.' They were particularly struck by the temple's享 hall — 'The hall is covered with yellow glazed tiles, its platform in three tiers.' This hall, eleven bays wide, is one of the largest Ming timber structures outside the Forbidden City. Inside, sixty-eight giant columns are all made of golden-thread nanmu — 'trees that require both arms to encircle, without paint or lacquer, the wood grain shining brightly' — that natural wood texture is more beautiful than any paint. When Liu Tong wrote about the sacrificial scene at the Imperial Ancestral Temple, his tone was solemn: 'Each year in the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months, and at year's end, the Son of Heaven conducts the rite in person.' What moved them most was: 'The ancient cypresses in the temple rise to the sky, all several hundred years old' — and these cypresses still stand today. The layout of the Imperial Ancestral Temple同样 conceals ritual principles: the front hall is the享 hall, the middle hall is the寝 hall, and the rear hall is the temple for远祖 — respectively housing ancestors of different generations. Outside the middle hall, fifteen side halls on east and west分别 house the spirits of meritorious imperial clansmen and ministers — 'accompanied by princes and ministers of merit, to manifest their virtue.' Though A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital does not elaborate, the 'eight-row dance in the courtyard' at the Imperial Ancestral Temple sacrifice — sixty-four people dancing in formation — along with the curling incense smoke and solemn bell and chime sounds, interwove to create the Ming dynasty's most magnificent royal sacrificial scene. At the year-end Grand Joint Sacrifice, the emperor led his ministers in the rite here — 'the rite is performed in the temple, and filial piety reaches heaven.'

stops.title: Stop 3: Imperial Academy and Confucian Temple — A Thousand-Year Cultural Thread of Left Temple, Right Academy
stops.content: The Imperial Academy and Beijing Confucian Temple each have their own chapters in A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital. Liu Tong wrote: 'The Imperial Academy is in the northeast of the city, built in the tenth year of the Yuan Dadе era, renovated during the Ming Yongle reign.' What most interested him about the Academy was the Biyong Hall — that square, double-eaved pavilion with a pointed roof, surrounded by water, where the emperor gave lectures. 'When the Son of Heaven comes to the Biyong to lecture, the students gather around the bridge-gate to listen, numbering in the thousands.' Adjacent, the Beijing Confucian Temple — the second largest Confucian temple in China — is the essence of 'left temple, right academy.' The Dacheng Hall, 'with double-eaved hip roof, nine bays wide,' is second only to the Forbidden City's Hall of Supreme Harmony in its等级. The 198 steles bearing the names of successful candidates in the imperial examinations — inscribed with the names of over fifty thousand jinshi from the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties — prompted Liu Tong's感叹: 'The steles stand like a forest, how flourishing it was.' Today, Guozijian Street is the only ancient street in Beijing that still preserves four memorial archways. Walking through the 'Chengsian Street' archway, ancient locust trees block out the sun — Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng might have walked just like this, discussing how to write the next chapter. Within the Imperial Academy is another cultural treasure not to be missed — the 'Thirteen Classics Stone Steles' carved during the Qianlong reign, 190 steles inscribed with the complete Confucian canon, one of the largest stone carving projects of the Qing dynasty. And the famous 'Traitor-Detecting Cypress' in the Confucian Temple — according to legend, when Ming dynasty treacherous prime minister Yan Song represented the emperor in worshipping Confucius, as he reached the tree, a branch suddenly knocked off his black gauze cap — though Liu Tong did not record this tale, it has been passed down in the alleys near the Academy to this day. Strolling along Chengsian Street, with the deep shade of ancient locusts and the towering archways, you can almost hear the sonorous chanting of scholars drifting out from the Yilun Hall of old.

stops.title: Stop 4: Lugou Bridge — The Vigil of Five Hundred Stone Lions
stops.content: Lugou Bridge receives considerable attention in A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital. Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng did not merely pass by — they made a special trip to count the lions. 'The stone railings of Lugou Bridge are carved with countless lions, large and small, beyond count.' — 'beyond count' indicates they could not tally them either. What they most admired was the moonlight scene of Lugou Bridge — 'Lugou Moonlight at Dawn' had already been one of the Eight Great Views of Yanjing in the Ming dynasty. 'The moonlight fills the sky, the water meets the sky, the strategic pass crouches like a tiger, the long bridge lies like a dragon' — sixteen characters painted a magnificent picture of a northern moonlit night. Emperor Qianlong later personally inscribed the 'Lugou Moonlight at Dawn' stele, which still stands at the east bridgehead. Liu Tong also recorded a folk legend: 'On the day the bridge was completed, a white crane descended from the clouds, hence the name Lugou.' — though fanciful, the beauty of it is real. The two scholars walked on the bridge, counting the countless stone lions, discussing the inscriptions on the steles — such was the leisurely and poetic life of Ming dynasty literati. Lugou Bridge is equally famous in the West — the 13th-century Venetian traveler Marco Polo described it in detail in his travels, calling it 'the finest stone bridge in the world,' and it is still known as the 'Marco Polo Bridge' to Westerners. Wanping County, at the bridge's eastern end, was built during the Ming Chongzhen era to defend the capital, forming a pincer with Lugou Bridge. On July 7, 1937, gunfire on Lugou Bridge ignited the flames of all-out national resistance — the 'July Seventh Incident' transformed this ancient bridge's image from poetic to solemn. Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng could not have imagined that the ancient bridge they wrote of as 'moonlight fills the sky, the long bridge lies like a dragon' would become a symbol of national awakening three centuries later. The stone lions on the bridge remain countless — they know everything, but they do not speak.

stops.title: Stop 5: Fayuan Temple — The Lilac Affairs of the Tang Dynasty Minzhong Temple
stops.content: Fayuan Temple is one of Beijing's oldest famous temples, founded in the nineteenth year of the Tang Zhenguan era (645), originally named Minzhong Temple — built to mourn the fallen soldiers of the eastern campaign. A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital records Fayuan Temple's origins: 'The temple has two Tang stelae, both describing the campaign against Liao.' Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng saw those Tang stelae and praised 'the strength of the calligraphy.' In the Ming dynasty, Fayuan Temple was famous for its lilacs — every spring when the lilacs bloomed, the capital's literati would gather here to admire the flowers and compose poetry. Liu Tong wrote: 'The lilacs in the temple are the finest in the capital. When they bloom, it is like purple clouds covering the temple.' That spectacle of 'purple clouds covering the temple' remains the most beautiful moment at Fayuan Temple to this day. In modern times, Fayuan Temple gained greater fame through Taiwan writer Li Ao's Beijing Fayuan Temple. In the novel, figures of the Hundred Days' Reform such as Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao, and Tan Sitong hold secret meetings at Fayuan Temple — but when Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng came, it was still a quiet Zen temple, lilacs swaying in the spring breeze, a monk sweeping beneath the flowers, just as it was written in the book. Fayuan Temple also holds a hidden Liao dynasty legend — in the third year of the Qingning era (1057), a great earthquake struck Youzhou, nearly destroying the city walls, and the main body of Minzhong Temple collapsed almost entirely, only the Tang-dynasty Guanyin Pavilion miraculously surviving. Emperor Daozong of Liao ordered its reconstruction and renamed it Great Minzhong Temple, on an unprecedented scale. In the spring of 1924, Indian poet Rabindranath Tagore, accompanied by Xu Zhimo, came to Fayuan Temple to admire the lilacs — the lilacs were like snow, and Tagore lingered among them, while Xu Zhimo recited poetry impromptu — a celebrated episode in Republican-era literary circles. Every April, the Fayuan Temple lilac poetry gathering takes place as scheduled — from Liu Tong's time to the present, the lilacs bloom every year, and poetry is written every year.

stops.title: Stop 6: Changchun Temple and Biyun Temple — Two Pure Lands North and South of the Capital
stops.content: Changchun Temple was built by imperial order during the Ming Wanli era at the behest of Empress Dowager Li, mother of Emperor Shenzong, and was known as 'the foremost temple of the capital.' Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng described it as 'with deep halls and solemn Buddha statues' — a Ming imperial temple of a grandeur unmatched by ordinary monasteries. The yellow glazed tiles on the Mahavira Hall gleamed in the sun — a color reserved for the imperial family. In the western outskirts of Beijing, at the foot of Fragrant Hills, Biyun Temple offers a different style — built against the mountain, rising层层, it is a perfect blend of garden and temple. A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital writes: 'The temple is in the Western Hills, set amid deep forests and valleys.' Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng most admired Biyun Temple's Diamond Throne Pagoda — its unique tower form, blending Han and Tibetan styles, is hard to find elsewhere in Beijing. The two temples, one south and one north — Changchun Temple close to the mortal world's烟火, Biyun Temple enjoying the tranquility of mountain forests. The Beijing of Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng was woven from such distinctive historic sites. They knew these buildings would eventually age, collapse, and be forgotten — but as long as A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital exists, they will never disappear. Changchun Temple once housed a Ming dynasty glazed Buddha statue — bronze-cast with a gold-infiltrated surface, exquisitely crafted. A Brief Account of the Scenery of the Imperial Capital records: 'The statue was three zhang tall, solemn and wonderful.' Sadly, the giant statue was lost in the wars at the end of the Qing dynasty. The surviving painting 'Tea Distribution at Changchun Temple' by Mi Wanzhong records the warm scene of tea distribution before the temple in those days: under ancient locust trees, steam rose from the tea, and all, noble or humble, could receive a bowl of nectar. Biyun Temple续写着 new legends — in 1925, after Sun Yat-sen's death, his coffin was temporarily housed in the Diamond Throne Pagoda, and today the pagoda contains his cenotaph. The five hundred colored clay arhat figures in the Arhat Hall each have distinct expressions — 'the statues are like living people, their joys and angers一一 distinguishable.' The lilacs of Fayuan Temple, the arhats of Biyun Temple — Liu Tong and Yu Yizheng's Beijing is as rich as this: with the solemnity of the Buddha and the warmth of humanity.
